title: Why You Overvalue What You Already Own: The $7 Mug Experiment
alt_title_1: Kahneman & Thaler's $7 vs $3.50 Mug Test Explained
alt_title_2: Beat the Endowment Effect With One Simple Cash Test
description_hook: In a famous 1990 Journal of Political Economy experiment at Cornell, Daniel Kahneman, Jack Knetsch, and Richard Thaler proved that owning a simple coffee mug for minutes doubled its perceived value (~$7 vs ~$3.50). Apply the Cash-Equivalent Test to clear portfolio clutter.

affiliate_cta.pinned_comment: What stock, subscription, or project are you holding right now purely because you already own it? Grab our Cash-Equivalent Decision Matrix here: https://kenvh0010-lang.github.io/admin/bio/

scenes.headline: Five Minutes of Ownership Doubles Perceived Value
scenes.stat_label: SELLERS' DEMAND VS BUYERS' OFFER FOR THE SAME MUG
bullets: Same university mug, inspected by the same students
Mere possession split perceived value roughly 2-to-1
scenes.narration: Hand someone an ordinary coffee mug for five minutes, and they instantly value it at roughly double what an identical stranger will pay.
scenes.source: Kahneman, Knetsch & Thaler, Journal of Political Economy (1990)

scenes.headline: Cornell's 1990 Coffee Mug Experiment
bullets: Randomly gifted mug owners asked ~$7 to part with it
Non-owners were only willing to pay ~$3.50 to acquire it
scenes.narration: In a classic 1990 Journal of Political Economy experiment at Cornell, Daniel Kahneman, Jack Knetsch, and Richard Thaler found mug owners demanded around seven dollars to sell, while buyers offered near three-fifty.
scenes.source: Kahneman, Knetsch & Thaler, 'Experimental Tests of the Endowment Effect', JPE (1990)

scenes.headline: Holding Dead Weight Just Because It's Yours
scenes.left_body: Keeps lagging stocks & stalled projects out of attachment
scenes.right_body: Judges every position as if deciding from scratch in cash
scenes.narration: This Endowment Effect quietly clogs your portfolio and home: you cling to underperforming stocks, stalled projects, and unused gear simply because they are already yours.

scenes.headline: Run the Cash-Equivalent Test
scenes.stat_label: WOULD YOU BUY IT TODAY WITH FRESH CASH?
scenes.stat_subtext: Reallocate trapped capital into higher-compounding assets
scenes.narration: Break ownership bias with the Cash-Equivalent Test: ask yourself, if I held this asset's market value in cash today, would I buy it again right now?

scenes.headline: Cut Attachment and Redeploy Capital
bullets: Audit holdings and subscriptions as a fresh cash buyer
Exit anything you would refuse to purchase today
scenes.narration: If the honest answer is no, sell the dead weight and redeploy your capital where it compounds.
scenes.source: Mind & Margin rule of thumb based on Kahneman, Knetsch & Thaler (1990)
